column2: For each product, the monthly report says how much was made, how much was sold and at what price.
Sales money = number sold × price per unit.
Banks, insurers, leasing companies and contractors have a different kind of monthly report.
A shoe shop: this month it sold 200 pairs at 1 million each; the month’s sales are 200 million.
Ask where the sales growth came from: selling more, or selling at higher prices (inflation and the dollar)?
Compare each month with the same month last year, because some businesses are seasonal; for example, cement sells less in winter.
If it produces more than it sells for several months in a row, goods pile up in the warehouse.
You don’t compare ice-cream sales in Dey with Mordad; you compare this Dey with last Dey.
The monthly report only shows sales, not costs.
To see whether profit per unit went up, compare the selling price with the raw-material price.
The gap between these two prices is the best sign of profit between two quarterly reports.
If a baker sells bread 10% dearer but flour got 30% dearer, their profit went down, not up.
A company must post important news on Codal immediately.
Group A: news with a direct, large effect on the price; usually the ticker is halted first and then the news comes out.
Group B: news with a smaller or indirect effect.
Like family news: “Dad changed jobs” is very important; “we bought a new fridge” less so.
1. How much money? Compare the amount with the company’s yearly profit from its main work. Under 5% usually doesn’t matter.
2. Once, or every year? Selling land happens once; a new production line brings profit every year.
3. Real money, or a number on paper? A real sale is different from revaluing an asset.
Getting a bonus once is different from getting a raise; the second repeats every month.
This news really changes profit:
Raw materials, power and gas getting dearer or cheaper; a change in the price the government sets for the product.
A new production line starting, or production stopping because of an accident or power cuts.
A very large contract, a change in the government’s share of a mine, or a big tax penalty.
For a taxi, a rise in petrol prices or a licence for a new route really changes income; changing the car’s colour doesn’t.
In this report managers say what they plan for the rest of the year: how much they’ll produce and sell, raw-material prices, project progress, staff numbers and risks.
An important exercise: compare last year’s promises with this year’s results.
A manager who says every year “the project will be finished next year” is less believable.
Like a builder who says every month “the building will be done next month”; after three times, you don’t believe them any more.
Before the meeting, the board reports on the year’s work.
Two parts matter most: deals with companies and people close to the managers or the main owner, and the proposed cash dividend.
If the building manager gave the repairs to their brother’s company, you need to see whether the price was fair.

A capital increase has several stages: the board’s proposal and justification report, the auditor’s opinion, the Exchange Organisation’s permit, approval at the meeting, then carrying it out and registering it.
In the justification report find three numbers: how much the project costs, how much extra profit it brings each year once running, and when it starts running.
Like when a shop’s partners want to put in money and take the shop next door too: they need to know what it costs, how much extra income it brings and from when.
Capital increases come from different places, and not all of them bring in new money.
Cash contributions: shareholders put in fresh money. If it’s spent on a good project it creates value; if it’s spent on debt, everyone’s share just gets smaller.
From retained earnings: no new money comes in; profit that wasn’t paid out is just spent on a project.
From revaluation: no money comes in at all; only the number of shares goes up.
If you cut a pizza into 8 slices instead of 4, the pizza doesn’t get bigger; a capital increase from revaluation is just that.
The annual meeting is held at most 4 months after the end of the financial year and approves the dividend per share (DPS).
By law at least 10% of net profit must be paid out, and payment must be made within 8 months of the meeting.
On the day the ticker reopens after the meeting, the share price drops by the amount of that dividend; so buying just before the meeting, only for the dividend, gains you nothing in itself.
If a company borrows to pay the dividend, or waits until the last day of the deadline, its cash is weak.
Like taking 10,000 tomans out of a piggy bank with 100,000: the money reached you, but the piggy bank is also 10,000 lighter.
The dividend goes to whoever owns the share on the day of the meeting.
According to Dr. Khosravani, small shareholders usually get their dividend before the legal deadline.
Like a company’s New Year bonus: it goes to whoever is on staff the day it’s approved, even if it’s paid the next month.
